statement: Scholars disagree over whether Genesis 1 shows specific literary engagement with Enūma Eliš or instead draws from a broader ancient West Asian cosmological environment; direct borrowing from Enūma Eliš is not established.
scholarly_disagreement: David M. Carr argues that Genesis 1 shows particular engagement with Enūma Eliš, while Alexander Heidel and others regard direct dependence as unproven and leave broader shared background or other precursors open.

sources.citation: David M. Carr, The Formation of Genesis 1–11: Biblical and Other Precursors (Oxford University Press, 2020), ch. 1, “Precursors to the Priestly Creation Account (Gen 1:1–2:3).”
sources.author: David M. Carr
sources.access_note: Oxford abstract states that Carr builds a case for particular engagement with Enūma Eliš and then considers additional biblical and nonbiblical precursors.

sources.citation: Alexander Heidel, The Babylonian Genesis: The Story of Creation, 2nd ed. (University of Chicago Press, 1963; orig. 1951).
sources.author: Alexander Heidel
sources.access_note: University of Chicago scan concludes that incontrovertible evidence for or against dependence could not be produced and leaves the question open.

interpretations.position: Genesis 1 shows specific engagement with Enūma Eliš as part of its formation.
interpretations.strongest_case: The Priestly account can be read as responding to a recognizable Mesopotamian creation tradition in an exilic/post-exilic scribal setting.

interpretations.position: The similarities do not demonstrate direct dependence on Enūma Eliš and may reflect broader ancient West Asian background or multiple precursors.
interpretations.strongest_case: Differences are substantial and shared motifs are not unique to Enūma Eliš, so a unique source-target dependence cannot be established from resemblance alone.

does_not_demonstrate: This does not establish that Genesis 1 copied Enūma Eliš.
This does not establish a unique Babylonian source for every Genesis 1 motif.
This does not convert motif similarity into a transmission claim without the cited scholarly argument.
adversarial_counter: The same motifs occur across multiple ancient West Asian traditions, and chronology/contact opportunity alone cannot identify a unique source.
notes: Backs a DISPUTED UNCERTAIN_CONNECTION edge, not BORROWING.
